opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, when we first heard TensorFlow was coming, there was a moment of "well, is this still worth doing?" Google has a huge team, a lot of resources, and they'd obviously put a lot of engineering behind it. But a few things made us feel it was still worth pursuing.

First, MXNet didn't come out of nowhere. It grew out of a community of people who had already been building things like CXXNet, Minerva, and Purine. We had our own ideas about how a deep learning system should be designed, like combining imperative and symbolic programming, being memory-efficient, and scaling across multiple GPUs and machines. Those were real technical questions we cared about, and they didn't go away just because another big framework was launching.

Second, I've always believed it's healthy for the ecosystem to have more than one approach, especially open, community-driven ones. A lot of interesting innovation happens when different groups try different design choices and learn from each other. If everyone just waits for one big company to define everything, you lose some of that diversity.

And third, at a personal level, building the system was how I learned. Even if MXNet didn't "win," the experience of designing the computation graph, the memory planning, the distributed parts, all of that shaped how I think about machine learning systems. A lot of what I did later, like TVM and the compiler work, really grew out of lessons from that period.

So it wasn't really about beating TensorFlow. It was more that we had ideas we wanted to explore, a community that was excited about them, and we thought the open-source world would be better with that option available.

r001.rationale: The response says MXNet grew out of earlier projects, but does not state that it was proposed before Chen knew TensorFlow was forthcoming.

r002.rationale: It says MXNet had its own design ideas, including combining imperative and symbolic programming, and that these differences made it worth pursuing despite TensorFlow’s arrival.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, we knew TensorFlow was coming before it came out, and we knew Google was going to put a lot of resources behind it. So the question wasn't really whether we could out-resource Google—we obviously couldn't. The question was whether there was still something worth saying.

And we felt there was. MXNet came out of a few of us merging projects—CXXNet, Minerva, Purine—and we had been thinking a lot about one specific design question: how do you let people mix imperative, NumPy-style programming with declarative, symbolic graphs in the same system? At the time Theano and then TensorFlow were very much on the symbolic side, and Torch was on the imperative side. We thought the right answer was both, and that you'd need the engine underneath to schedule across them. That was a real technical bet, not just "let's build another framework."

The other thing was efficiency, especially memory. A lot of us were students with limited GPUs. Being able to train a bigger model on a single card, or run on a phone, or scale across machines with a parameter server without rewriting things—those mattered to us in a way they maybe didn't matter to a company with unlimited hardware.

And I think there's a more personal reason too. If you only work on things where you're certain you'll win, you'll never work on anything interesting. Even if MXNet didn't become the dominant framework, the ideas would get out. And a lot of them did—the imperative-plus-symbolic idea, the memory optimizations, the compilation ideas that later became TVM. So I don't regret it. It was a good vehicle for learning what a deep learning system should look like, and for the community that grew around it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says they knew TensorFlow was coming before its release, but does not say MXNet was proposed before they learned that.

r002.rationale: The candidate says MXNet was worth pursuing because it aimed to combine imperative NumPy-style programming with declarative symbolic graphs, which it presents as a distinct design bet.

astra-6.text:
At the time, we had already started working on MXNet. When we heard TensorFlow was coming, the question was really, do we still have something useful to contribute? I felt the answer was yes. There were different ideas worth exploring about how to build a deep learning system, and having one framework from a large company didn’t mean those questions were settled.

For me, it was also an opportunity to learn by building, together with an open-source community. So it wasn’t necessarily about beating TensorFlow. It was about pursuing ideas we believed in and seeing whether they could be useful to people.

We felt there was still room to explore different ideas in a deep learning framework, particularly around efficiency, distributed training, and flexibility. Learning that TensorFlow was coming didn’t make those problems disappear. It was an opportunity to keep learning and see whether our approach could offer something useful. You don’t have to be the only framework to make a meaningful contribution.
